title: That Golden Era
paragraphs: In the Hindu temples, the presiding deity has two statues - mūlavar, the stone statue fixed inside sanctum sanctorum and uṟcavar , the statue made of five types of metals. Of them, mūlavar is worshipped in the place of its location, whereas uṟcavar is taken in procession outside the temple, as the representative of mūlavar during festivals.

This practice is seen observed in all the temples of Tamiḻnāṭu. But the exceptions are the six temples at Tiruvārūr and the adjoining Tirukkuvaḷai, Tirukkōpuravāsal, Tirumaṟaikkāṭu, Tirunākai and Tiruvāymūr, where the mūlavar and uṟcavar statues are not made of stone and metal respectively, and they look alike. The same Tiyākarāja statue is fixed in the sanctum sanctorum and taken in procession also. It is also used in chariot processions. In these shrines, the procession deity has a more pronounced honour of worship.

The devotees and priests carry the statue on their shoulders every year on auspicious days to mark the advent of the festival. They place it on a chariot and celebrate festivals drawing the chariots. At the culmination of the festivals, the statue is reinstated inside the temple.
In the uḻiñai situation of puṟam poetry, Tolkāppiyam Poruḷatikāram speaks of a similar honour accorded by kings to their victorious swords.

The uḻiñai puṟam situation deals with the siege of an enemy fort by a king and the defence of the fort by the king remaining within. The siege is resorted to when the authority of the attacking king is defied by the other.
Both the kings at the start of the war place their swords under the decorated canopy at an auspicious hour and take them in procession.

The soldiers defending the fort from inside and the ones attacking it from outside wage a fierce war against each other, either standing on or climbing over the ladders made of wooden planks which are placed on the fort walls.

The spectacle of the soldiers inside and outside the fort fighting each other and retreating resembles the joining and moving away of the parasitic plant in the moat around the fort wall due to the strong winds or the vibration caused by the deed of war.
The battle extends to many parts of the town too.

Not completely relying upon the soldiers from both the sides and in order to demonstrate the steely resolve of their hearts, the warring kings fight on the wall of the fort themselves, without ever worrying about their lives.
After all, the garland of victory is meant for only one of them! Before the defeat could stare large on his face, a king saves his dignity by embracing death.
The purificatory ceremonies are performed for the sword of the victor king, as it is deemed to be responsible for his triumph.

It was the ethos of those days to hold aloft the white canopy over the sword and thereby pay obeisance to the sword, which sealed victory in the war by being the deity in the santorum and the procession deity. Yes, it was the era which recognized and honoured valour. In spite of being an era of wars, it certainly was the golden epoch hailing the greatness of the Tamiḻ race, in that the victor king was being honoured with coronation in the name of the deceased king. Is not this a mark of magnanimity of our ancestors? Look at the Tolkāppiyam verse:

> Uḻiñai marks twelve other substrands too: > Sending of the royal parasol and sword at an auspicious hour > Preceding the siege of the foe intended; > The raging fight of the soldiers > As they stand on ladders fitted to the fort; > The fierce, resolute battle > Intended to end the siege outside the fortress; > The mighty defence offered by the besieged within; > Breach of the defence by the besieging men; > Action in the moat of the fortress; > Carrying the battle thereon

> Into the town of the besieged; > Triumphant scaling of the fort within; > The ceremonial bath of the victorious king > And his taking the crown of the vanquished; > The ceremonial bath of the sword of the victor; > And the absolute surrender of the vanquished. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 13)
